questions.question: What does ISRO stand for?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian Space Research Organization**__.

__ 
 
• **Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO)** is the national space agency of India, responsible for the planning, execution, and development of space exploration and satellite programs. 
 
• It was established in **1969** by **Dr. Vikram Sarabhai**, who is considered the father of the Indian space program. 
 
• ISRO operates under the **Department of Space**, which comes directly under the **Prime Minister of India**. Its headquarters is located in **Bengaluru, Karnataka**. 
 
• The main objective of ISRO is to develop **space technology** and its application for various national tasks, such as communication, weather forecasting, navigation, and Earth observation. 
 
• ISRO is globally recognized for its cost-effective space missions, such as the **Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM)**, also known as **Mangalyaan**, which made India the first Asian nation to reach Mars and the first nation globally to do so in its maiden attempt. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
 
 
• **Option 1: Indian Scientific Research Organization** 
 
 
• This is an incorrect option. The name does not correspond to any existing scientific organization in India. 
 
• While scientific research is a focus of various institutions in India, ISRO is specifically dedicated to **space exploration and technology development**. 
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Indian Satellite Rocket Organization** 
 
 
• This is an incorrect option. ISRO is not limited to satellite and rocket development but encompasses broader aspects of **space technology and its applications**. 
 
• Although ISRO is known for its successful launch vehicles such as the **PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle)** and **GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle)**, its scope extends beyond this. 
 
 
 
• **Option 4: International Space Research Organization** 
 
 
• This is also incorrect. ISRO is a **national agency** of India, not an international organization. 
 
• However, ISRO collaborates with various international space agencies such as NASA, ESA, and Roscosmos for research and missions. 
 
 
 
• **ISRO’s Achievements:** 
 
 
• Successful launch of **Chandrayaan-1**, India’s first lunar probe, in **2008**. 
 
• Launch of **Mangalyaan** (Mars Orbiter Mission) in **2013**, making India the first Asian country to reach Mars. 
 
• Development of **NavIC**, India’s own navigation system, comparable to GPS. 
 
• GSLV Mk III’s successful launch, which is capable of carrying heavier payloads and was used for the **Chandrayaan-2** mission in **2019**. 
 
 
 
• **Future Missions:** 
 
 
• Planned launch of **Gaganyaan**, India’s first manned space mission. 
 
• Development of a reusable launch vehicle to reduce the cost of space missions.

questions.question: What is one of the following digital reforms was included under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for courts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Introduction of virtual court hearings**__.

__ 
 
• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita**, introduced as a replacement for the Indian Penal Code (IPC), includes provisions aimed at modernizing the judicial process in India. 
 
• A significant reform under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is the **introduction of virtual court hearings**, which ensures that judicial processes can continue seamlessly using technology. 
 
• Virtual hearings allow **litigants, lawyers, and judges** to participate in court proceedings without being physically present, thereby reducing delays and improving accessibility, particularly during emergencies like the COVID-19 pandemic. 
 
• These hearings are conducted using **secure digital platforms** to maintain the integrity and confidentiality of the judicial process. 
 
• The reform emphasizes **efficiency, transparency, and accessibility** by leveraging technology to reduce pendency in courts and make justice delivery more effective. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Digital Reforms for Courts:** 
 
 
• The Indian judiciary has been adopting digital reforms such as the **e-Courts Mission Mode Project**, which aims to computerize courts and enhance their functioning. 
 
• Virtual court hearings are part of this broader initiative, enabling remote access and reducing the time taken for proceedings. 
 
• Such reforms promote a paperless environment, improving efficiency and reducing costs. 
 
 
 
• **Impact of Virtual Hearings:** 
 
 
• Virtual hearings have made justice delivery more inclusive by allowing individuals from **remote and rural areas** to participate in proceedings without incurring significant travel expenses. 
 
• They are particularly beneficial for cases involving **environmental disasters, pandemics, or other emergencies**. 
 
 
 
• **Other Proposed Reforms Under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita:** 
 
 
• The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita emphasizes **streamlining procedures**, such as fast-tracking cases and introducing time limits for specific processes. 
 
• The focus on **using digital evidence** highlights the importance of technology in modern justice delivery. 
 
 
 
• **Technological Integration in Judiciary:** 
 
 
• Besides virtual hearings, the judiciary is exploring the use of tools like **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** for case management and legal research. 
 
• Other technological advancements include **online case filing, digital case records, and e-payment systems** for court fees. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Comparison of Other Options:** 
 
 
• **No trials allowed:** This is not a reform under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Trials remain an integral part of the judicial process. 
 
• **Online registration for judges:** While technology is used for administrative tasks, this specific option is not directly related to the reforms under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. 
 
• **Abolition of police reports:** This is incorrect as police reports (FIRs) are a critical part of the criminal justice system in India. 
 
 
 
• **Examples of Virtual Hearings:** 
 
 
• During the **COVID-19 pandemic**, the Supreme Court and several High Courts in India conducted virtual hearings to ensure continuity in justice delivery.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary literary source for the Gupta period?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Allahabad Pillar Inscription of Samudragupta**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Allahabad Pillar Inscription** is one of the most important literary sources for the **Gupta period**. It provides detailed information about the reign of **Samudragupta**, one of the greatest rulers of the Gupta Empire.

• It was composed by **Harisena**, the court poet and minister of Samudragupta, and is written in **Sanskrit** using the **Brahmi script**.

• The inscription glorifies the achievements, conquests, and administrative policies of **Samudragupta**, describing him as a great warrior, statesman, and patron of arts and culture.

• The Allahabad Pillar Inscription is located on a pillar at **Kausambi (near Allahabad)** and is a crucial source for understanding the political and military history of the Gupta Empire.

• It also mentions the **extent of Samudragupta's empire**, including his campaigns across northern and southern India, and his relations with other rulers and kingdoms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Nasik Prashasti of Gautamiputra Satakarni**: 

• The Nasik Prashasti was issued by **Gautamiputra Satakarni**, a ruler of the **Satavahana dynasty**. It provides information about his military achievements and administrative policies.

• It is an inscription found in the Nasik caves and predates the Gupta period, making it unrelated to the literary sources of the Gupta era.

• **Aihole Inscription of Pulakeshin II**: 

• The Aihole inscription was issued by **Pulakeshin II**, a ruler of the **Chalukya dynasty**. It describes his conquests and achievements.

• It belongs to the early medieval period and is not connected to the Gupta period.

• **Hathigumpha Inscription of Kharavela**: 

• The Hathigumpha inscription is attributed to **Kharavela**, a ruler of the **Kalinga dynasty**. It is engraved on a rock near Bhubaneswar, Odisha.

• This inscription predates the Gupta period and describes the achievements of Kharavela, making it unrelated to Gupta literary sources.

• **Samudragupta's Significance**: 

• Samudragupta is often referred to as the **Napoleon of India** due to his extensive military campaigns and ability to establish a vast empire.

• The Gupta Empire under Samudragupta witnessed significant advancements in **art, culture, and administration**, earning it the title of the **Golden Age of India**.

• The Allahabad Pillar Inscription is a primary source for understanding the extent of his empire, which stretched from **the Himalayas to the southern tip of India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Gupta Period**: The Gupta Empire (circa 320-550 CE) is known for its contributions to **literature, science, mathematics, astronomy, and art**. The Allahabad Pillar Inscription is a testament to its historical richness.

• **Samudragupta's Conquests**: The inscription mentions his conquests over numerous kingdoms, including **northern India** and parts of southern India, showcasing his military prowess.

• **Court Poet Harisena**: Harisena's composition of the inscription highlights the importance of royal patronage of **literature and scholarship** during the Gupta era.

**Assertion (A)**: The retreating monsoon winds are associated with dry weather and clear skies in northern India.

**Reason (R)**: During the retreating monsoon, the low-pressure area over the northern plains is replaced by a high-pressure system.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Assertion (A):** The retreating monsoon winds are associated with **dry weather and clear skies** in northern India. 
 
 
• This statement is **correct**. During the retreating monsoon phase (typically from October to November), the southwest monsoon winds withdraw from the Indian subcontinent. 
 
• As the moist monsoon winds retreat, they no longer bring rainfall to northern India, leading to **clear skies and dry weather conditions**. 
 
 

• **Reason (R):** During the retreating monsoon, the **low-pressure area** over the northern plains is replaced by a **high-pressure system**. 
 
 
• This statement is also **correct**. As the monsoon withdraws, the low-pressure system that dominated during the rainy season dissipates, and a high-pressure system takes its place. 
 
• The high-pressure system results in **subsidence of air**, which suppresses cloud formation, causing clear skies and dry conditions. 
 
 

• **Explanation:** The Reason (R) correctly explains the Assertion (A). 
 
 
• The retreating monsoon is characterized by the withdrawal of moist winds and the establishment of high-pressure systems in northern India, resulting in **clear skies and dry weather**. 
 
• This phenomenon marks the transition from the monsoon season to the winter season in India. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Retreating Monsoon:** 
 
 
• The retreating monsoon occurs during **October and November**, marking the transition from the rainy season to winter in India. 
 
• It is characterized by the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon winds and the establishment of dry, northeast trade winds. 
 
• The retreating monsoon is most prominent in regions like **North India, the Western Ghats, and Tamil Nadu**, where it often brings light showers. 
 
 

• **High-Pressure Systems:** 
 
 
• A high-pressure system forms when air converges aloft and descends, causing **subsidence** (downward movement of air). 
 
• This results in **clear skies, low humidity, and dry weather**, typical of post-monsoon conditions in northern India. 
 
 

• **Impact on Tamil Nadu:** 
 
 
• While northern India experiences dry weather during the retreating monsoon, Tamil Nadu receives significant rainfall due to the **northeast monsoon winds**. 
 
• This phenomenon is known as the **northeast monsoon season**, which is crucial for agricultural activities in Tamil Nadu. 
 
 

• **Climatological Significance:** 
 
 
• The retreating monsoon period is critical for the onset of the **Rabi crop season** in India, as the dry weather provides favorable conditions for sowing. 
 
• This period also marks the beginning of a reduction in humidity and a gradual drop in temperatures in northern India. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Weather Patterns:** The retreating monsoon is marked by **clear skies, reduced rainfall, and cooler nights**, especially in northern and central India. 

• **Seasonal Transition:** This phase represents a transition from the wet monsoon season to the dry winter season, with significant changes in wind patterns and atmospheric pressure. 

• **Regional Variations:** While northern and central India experience dry weather, southern states like Tamil Nadu benefit from the **northeast monsoon**, which brings rainfall. 

• **Temperature Changes:** The retreating monsoon is often accompanied by a drop in night temperatures, leading to a cooler climate in many regions.

questions.question: **Fill in the blanks**: A Bill that "imposes a new tax" is categorised at the Centre as a ______ Bill.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Money Bill**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 
__ 
 
• A **Money Bill** is a type of bill in the Indian Parliament that exclusively deals with matters specified in **Article 110** of the Constitution of India. 
 
• It includes provisions for the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of any **tax or revenue** collection. 
 
• Under Article 110, a bill is classified as a Money Bill if it deals with: 
 
 
• The imposition or abolition of taxes. 
 
• The custody and withdrawal of money from the **Consolidated Fund of India** or the **Contingency Fund of India**. 
 
• The appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund. 
 
 
 
• A Money Bill can only be introduced in the **Lok Sabha**, not in the Rajya Sabha. 
 
• After being passed by the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha can only suggest amendments, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. The Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend a Money Bill without the concurrence of the Lok Sabha. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Ordinary Bill:** 
 
 
• An Ordinary Bill is a regular bill that deals with any matter other than financial matters specified under Article 110. 
 
• It can be introduced in either the **Lok Sabha** or the **Rajya Sabha**. 
 
• It requires the approval of both houses and has no special financial provisions. 
 
 
 
• **Private Bill:** 
 
 
• A Private Bill is introduced by a **private member** (a Member of Parliament who is not a minister). 
 
• It deals with public interest issues but is rarely passed in the Indian Parliament. 
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Amendment Bill:** 
 
 
• It is introduced to amend the provisions of the **Constitution of India** under Article 368. 
 
• It requires a special majority in both houses of Parliament and, in some cases, the ratification of half of the state legislatures. 
 
 
 
• **Procedure for a Money Bill:** 
 
 
• The Speaker of the Lok Sabha decides whether a bill is a Money Bill or not, and the decision is final. 
 
• After passage in the Lok Sabha, the Money Bill is sent to the Rajya Sabha, which must return it within **14 days**. 
 
• If the Rajya Sabha fails to return the bill within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both houses in the form in which it was passed by the Lok Sabha. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Article 110:** It lays down the definition of a Money Bill in the Indian Constitution. 
 
• **Role of the Speaker:** The Speaker of the Lok Sabha has the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill or not. 
 
• **Exclusive Introduction:** Money Bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha on the recommendation of the **President of India**. 
 
• **Examples:** The **Finance Bill** and the **Appropriation Bill** are types of Money Bills.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a rigid body about an axis:

options.text: Is a scalar quantity, independent of the axis
Is a vector quantity, dependent on the axis
Is a scalar quantity, dependent on the axis
Is a tensor quantity, independent of the axis

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Is a scalar quantity, dependent on the axis**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• The **moment of inertia** of a rigid body is a measure of its resistance to angular acceleration when a torque is applied about an axis. 

• **Moment of inertia** is a scalar quantity and depends on the **distribution of mass** in the rigid body and the **specific axis** about which it is being calculated. 

• It is calculated mathematically as the **integral of mass elements multiplied by the square of their perpendicular distances** from the axis of rotation (**I = ∫r² dm**). 

• The value of the moment of inertia changes based on the **geometry, shape, and orientation** of the body relative to the axis. For example, the moment of inertia of a rod about its center is different from that about one of its ends. 

• *Hence, the moment of inertia is a scalar quantity, but it is **dependent on the axis**.* 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Definition of Moment of Inertia:** 
 

• The moment of inertia represents the rotational equivalent of mass in linear motion. It quantifies how the mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation. 

• Its SI unit is **kg.m²**, and it is always a positive scalar quantity. 
 
 

• **Factors Affecting Moment of Inertia:** 
 

• **Mass Distribution:** The farther the mass is from the axis, the greater the moment of inertia. 

• **Axis of Rotation:** The axis's location and orientation significantly affect the value of the moment of inertia. For example, a uniform disc has different moments of inertia when rotated about its central axis and its diameter. 

• **Shape and Geometry:** The shape (sphere, cylinder, rod, etc.) of the object influences its moment of inertia. 
 
 

• **Applications of Moment of Inertia:** 
 

• It is crucial in **mechanical systems** involving rotation, such as flywheels and turbines. 

• In the design of vehicles, it helps determine the **stability and control** of rotating components like wheels and propellers. 

• It is also used in **structural engineering** to analyze beams and other elements subject to torque or rotational forces. 
 
 

• **Parallel and Perpendicular Axis Theorems:** 
 

• **Parallel Axis Theorem:** If the moment of inertia of a body about an axis passing through its center of mass is known, the moment of inertia about any parallel axis can be calculated as **I = I_cm + Md²**, where d is the distance between the axes. 

• **Perpendicular Axis Theorem:** For a planar body, the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plane is the sum of the moments of inertia about two mutually perpendicular axes in the plane. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Moment of Inertia for Common Shapes:** 
 

• **Thin Rod:** About an axis through the center and perpendicular to its length: **I = (1/12)ML²**. 

• **Solid Sphere:** About its diameter: **I = (2/5)MR²**. 

• **Solid Cylinder:** About its central axis: **I = (1/2)MR²**. 

• **Hollow Cylinder:** About its central axis: **I = MR²**. 
 
 

• The **moment of inertia** is an integral property that underpins key concepts in rotational dynamics, such as angular momentum and torque. 

• It is not a vector quantity but a scalar, although its influence is directional based on the axis of rotation. 

• Understanding the moment of inertia is essential in designing efficient mechanical systems and analyzing rotational motion in physics.

questions.question: Which of the following is another name for the revenue account of the government budget?

__ 
 
• **Revenue Budget** refers to the government’s accounting of its revenue receipts (both tax and non-tax) and the expenditure met from this revenue. 
 
• It includes all recurring income sources such as **tax revenues** (e.g., income tax, GST, corporate tax) and **non-tax revenues** (e.g., dividends from public sector enterprises, interest receipts). 
 
• The revenue budget details the government’s recurring expenditures on areas such as **administration, subsidies, pensions, interest payments, and defense expenditure**. 
 
• When revenue receipts exceed revenue expenditure, it results in a **Revenue Surplus**. Conversely, when the expenditure surpasses receipts, it leads to a **Revenue Deficit**. 
 
• It differs from the **Capital Budget**, which deals with long-term investments and liabilities, focusing on creating assets like infrastructure. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Capital Budget:** 
 
 
• Deals with the government’s revenue from loans, borrowings, and the creation of assets like roads, schools, and hospitals. 
 
• Includes capital receipts (e.g., loans, recovery of loans, disinvestment) and capital expenditure (e.g., infrastructure development). 
 
 
 
• **Finance Budget:** 
 
 
• It refers to the overall annual financial statement presented in Parliament, containing details of both revenue and capital budgets. 
 
• It is an umbrella term encompassing all aspects of the government’s financial planning. 
 
 
 
• **Expenditure Budget:** 
 
 
• It is a part of the Union Budget that provides a detailed account of the government’s expenditure for the fiscal year. 
 
• It is divided into revenue expenditure and capital expenditure. 
 
 
 
• **Revenue Receipts:** 
 
 
• Comprises tax revenues (e.g., GST, customs duties) and non-tax revenues (e.g., dividends, interest receipts). 
 
• These receipts do not lead to an increase in liabilities or a reduction in assets. 
 
 
 
• **Revenue Expenditure:** 
 
 
• Includes day-to-day operational expenses such as salaries, subsidies, and interest payments. 
 
• Unlike capital expenditure, it does not result in the creation of assets or reduction of liabilities. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Key Differences between Revenue and Capital Budget:** 
 
 
• **Revenue Budget:** Focuses on recurring income and expenditure, does not create assets. 
 
• **Capital Budget:** Focuses on long-term investments, asset creation, and liabilities. 
 
 
 
• **Revenue Deficit:** Occurs when revenue expenditure exceeds revenue receipts, indicating a shortfall in meeting day-to-day expenses. 
 
• **Budget Presentation:** In India, the Union Budget is presented annually by the Finance Minister, as mandated under **Article 112** of the Indian Constitution. 
 
• **Key Components of Union Budget:** Revenue Budget, Capital Budget, Finance Bill, and Appropriation Bill. 
 
• **Fiscal Responsibility:** The **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act** guides the government to reduce fiscal deficits and ensure fiscal discipline.

questions.question: Why did the Indian government resort to licensing even for expanding existing private sector industries under IPR 1956?

options.text: To keep production under government control

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To keep production under government control**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) of 1956** was a landmark in India’s economic policy, laying the foundation of a mixed economy where both the public and private sectors could co-exist under state regulation.
 
• The government introduced licensing even for expansion of private industries to maintain **control over production capacity** and ensure that resources were allocated based on national priorities.
 
• The licensing system aimed to regulate the growth of certain industries, ensuring that they aligned with the **development goals of the government**, such as equitable distribution of resources and prevention of monopolies.
 
• This measure was implemented to ensure that the private sector did not dominate critical industries and that the state maintained a significant role in economic planning and resource allocation.
 
• The focus was particularly on industries considered critical for national development, such as **steel, heavy machinery, and defense**, which were placed under stringent control to meet long-term goals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) of 1956:**
 
 
• The IPR 1956 categorized industries into three schedules:
 
 
• **Schedule A:** Industries exclusively reserved for the public sector, such as defense and atomic energy.
 
• **Schedule B:** Industries where both the public and private sectors could operate, but the government took an active role.
 
• **Schedule C:** Industries left to the private sector but regulated by the government through licensing.
 
 
 
• The policy emphasized the importance of the public sector in commanding the economy and achieving **socialist-inspired goals** of equitable distribution of wealth.
 
 
 
• **Objectives of Licensing:**
 
 
• To prevent excessive concentration of economic power in a few hands and ensure **balanced regional development**.
 
• To prioritize the allocation of resources to industries crucial for the country’s development, such as infrastructure and heavy industries.
 
• To regulate production to meet domestic demands and prevent overproduction or underproduction in specific sectors.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Licensing:**
 
 
• The licensing system led to the emergence of the **License Raj**, where businesses had to obtain multiple clearances and approvals, often leading to inefficiencies and corruption.
 
• While the system aimed to ensure equitable growth, it also hindered innovation and competitiveness in the private sector.
 
• The government retained significant control over industrial growth, aligning production with its planned economic goals.
 
 
 
• **Alternatives to Licensing:**
 
 
• In the 1991 economic reforms, the government dismantled the License Raj, allowing industries to grow freely with fewer restrictions.
 
• This liberalization policy aimed to boost **economic efficiency, innovation, and competitiveness** in the global market.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1: To promote export competition:** This is incorrect. Licensing was not aimed at promoting exports but at regulating industrial growth domestically.
 
• **Option 3: To prevent technological innovation:** This is incorrect. Licensing was not intended to hinder innovation but to ensure government control over critical industries.
 
• **Option 4: To encourage luxury production:** This is incorrect. The focus was on essential industries, not luxury goods, to meet the developmental needs of the country.

2. The Council can investigate inter-state disputes.

3. Its composition includes PM and Union Ministers.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**4) 2 and 3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Article 263 of the Constitution of India empowers the President, not Parliament, to establish the Inter-State Council. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The **Inter-State Council** is tasked with investigating and discussing subjects of common interest between states or between the Union and states. It also makes recommendations for better coordination of policy and action on such subjects. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• The composition of the **Inter-State Council** includes the **Prime Minister as the Chairperson**, Union Ministers, and Chief Ministers of states. It is structured to ensure representation from all levels of government. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• The Council's role is consultative, and it does not have adjudicatory or binding decision-making power over inter-state disputes.
 
• **Article 263** does not mandate the creation of an Inter-State Council but leaves it to the discretion of the President, based on the necessity for coordination and cooperation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Constitutional Provision (Article 263):**

 
 
• Article 263 of the Constitution provides for the establishment of an **Inter-State Council** to serve as a platform for discussion and resolution of disputes between states or between states and the Union.
 
• The article outlines three main purposes of the council: **investigating inter-state disputes, discussing subjects of common interest, and making recommendations** for coordination of policy and action.
 
• The Council is consultative in nature and does not have binding authority.
 
 
 
• **Composition of the Inter-State Council:**
 
 
• The **Prime Minister** serves as the Chairperson of the Council.
 
• Other members include **Chief Ministers of all states, Administrators of Union Territories, and Union Ministers** as designated by the Prime Minister.
 
 
 
• **Inter-State Council's Functions:**
 
 
• Facilitates coordination between states and the Union in areas of mutual interest.
 
• Provides recommendations for better policy implementation and dispute resolution.
 
• Investigates and discusses specific issues referred to it by the President.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Council:**
 
 
• Helps in promoting cooperative federalism by providing a platform for dialogue between states and the Union.
 
• Addresses administrative and legislative challenges in a non-adjudicative manner.
 
• Encourages harmonization of policies across states for common goals such as economic growth and social development.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The Inter-State Council was established in **1990** by a Presidential Order based on the recommendations of the **Sarkaria Commission**.
 
• The Sarkaria Commission emphasized the need for such a forum to improve Centre-State and inter-state relations.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of the Inter-State Council:** It is purely advisory in nature and does not have the power to adjudicate disputes or enforce its recommendations.
 
• **Sarkaria Commission:** Recommended the establishment of the Inter-State Council to address Centre-State and inter-state conflicts and enhance cooperative federalism.
 
• **Article 262 vs. Article 263:** While **Article 262** deals with the adjudication of inter-state water disputes, **Article 263** focuses on a consultative mechanism for broader inter-state issues.
 
• **Cooperative Federalism:** The council is an essential mechanism for fostering dialogue and collaboration between states and the Union, promoting the ideal of cooperative federalism enshrined in the Constitution.
